pumac-2018-geometry-b-01.title: Rotate the region
pumac-2018-geometry-b-01.body:
Put Fine Hall at the origin and Frist at $(-1,1)$. The region is $R=\{x>-1,\ y>1\}$ inside the disk of radius $5$. Rotating $R$ by $90^\circ,180^\circ,270^\circ$ about the origin gives four congruent regions that fit together like a pinwheel around the central square $[-1,1]^2$ and fill the rest of the disk. So
$$4\,[R]=25\pi-4,\qquad [R]=\frac{25}4\pi-1.$$
Thus $a=25$, $b=4$, $c=1$ and the answer is $30$.

**Answer: 30**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-01.title: Integrate
pumac-2018-geometry-b-01.body:
$[R]=\int_{-1}^{\sqrt{24}}\left(\sqrt{25-x^2}-1\right)dx$. An antiderivative of $\sqrt{25-x^2}$ is $\frac12\left(x\sqrt{25-x^2}+25\arcsin\frac x5\right)$. Since $\arcsin\frac{\sqrt{24}}5+\arcsin\frac15=\frac\pi2$, we get $[R]=\sqrt{24}+\frac{25\pi}4-\sqrt{24}-1=\frac{25}4\pi-1$.

**Answer: 30**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-02.title: Power of a point
pumac-2018-geometry-b-02.body:
Let $h$ be the height of the cone. The axis of the cone is a diameter of the sphere ($12$ long) through the apex, and the center of the base circle splits it into $h$ and $12-h$. The base circle is a chord-circle of the sphere, and a diameter of it has half-length $3$; by the intersecting chords theorem $3\cdot3=h(12-h)$, so $h^2-12h+9=0$ and $h=6\pm3\sqrt3$. Since $h>6$, $h=6+3\sqrt3$.

The volume is $\frac13\pi\cdot3^2\cdot h=3\pi(6+3\sqrt3)=\pi(9\sqrt3+18)$, so $a=9,b=3,c=18$ and the answer is $30$.

**Answer: 30**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-02.title: Distance from the center
pumac-2018-geometry-b-02.body:
The base plane is at distance $\sqrt{6^2-3^2}=3\sqrt3$ from the sphere's center. Since the height exceeds $6$, the apex is on the far side, so $h=6+3\sqrt3$, giving the same volume $\pi(9\sqrt3+18)$.

**Answer: 30**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-03.title: Similar triangles
pumac-2018-geometry-b-03.body:
Let $r$ be the radius. $\angle ABD=90^\circ$ (it subtends a diameter) and $BC\perp AD$, so $AB^2=AC\cdot AD=2r\cdot AC$.

The hypotenuse is $AB=4\sqrt{\tfrac12\cdot AC\cdot BC}$, so $AB^2=16\cdot\frac12\cdot AC\cdot30=240\,AC$. Therefore $2r\cdot AC=240\,AC$ and $r=120$.

**Answer: 120**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-04.title: Reflect in the angle bisector
pumac-2018-geometry-b-04.body:
$I$ and $E$ both lie on the bisector $AI$ of $\angle A$. Since $BI$ and $BE$ are the internal and external bisectors at $B$, $\angle IBE=90^\circ$; likewise $\angle ICE=90^\circ$. So $B$ and $C$ lie on the circle $\omega$ with diameter $IE$, as does $D$.

The center of $\omega$ is the midpoint of $IE$, which is on line $AI$, so reflection in $AI$ maps $\omega$ to itself and swaps lines $AB$ and $AC$. Line $AB$ meets $\omega$ at $B$ and $D$, so line $AC$ meets $\omega$ at the reflections $B'$ and $D'$; but line $AC$ meets $\omega$ at $C$ and at one other point, and $B'$ (with $AB'=17\neq AC$) is not $C$, so $D'=C$. Hence $AD=AC=\frac{70}3$ and $BD=\frac{70}3-17=\frac{19}3$. The answer is $19+3=22$.

**Answer: 22**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-04.title: Angle chase
pumac-2018-geometry-b-04.body:
In circle $\omega$, $\angle BDI=\angle BCI=\frac C2$ (same arc $BI$). In triangles $ADI$ and $ACI$: $\angle DAI=\angle CAI=\frac A2$, $\angle ADI=\angle ACI=\frac C2$, and $AI$ is common, so they are congruent and $AD=AC=\frac{70}3$. Then $BD=\frac{70}3-17=\frac{19}3$.

**Answer: 22**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-05.title: Coordinates
pumac-2018-geometry-b-05.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(30,0)$, $C=(30,60)$, $D=(0,60)$. Circle $T$: $x^2+y^2-60y=0$; circle $S$: $x^2+y^2-30x=0$. Subtracting gives $x=2y$, so $P=(24,12)$ and line $AP$ is $y=\frac x2$, meeting $BC$ ($x=30$) at $E=(30,15)$.

Tangents from $E$ to circle $T$ (center $(0,30)$, radius $30$): the line $BC$ itself ($x=30$) is one, and the other is the line through $E$ with slope $\frac34$: $3x-4y-30=0$ (distance from $(0,30)$ is $\frac{150}{5}=30$). It meets $AB$ ($y=0$) at $F=(10,0)$. So
$$[AEF]=\tfrac12\cdot AF\cdot BE=\tfrac12\cdot10\cdot15=75.$$

(The tangent $BC$ itself meets $AB$ at $F=B$, giving $[AEB]=\frac12\cdot30\cdot15=225$; the official key intends $F\neq B$ and gives $75$, noting $225$ as an unintended reading.)

**Answer: 75**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-06.title: Coordinates
pumac-2018-geometry-b-06.body:
Take $A=(0,0)$, $C=(12,0)$, $B=(0,4\sqrt3)$. The circumcircle $W$ has center $M=(6,2\sqrt3)$ (midpoint of $BC$) and radius $4\sqrt3$.

The point $D$ is on the ray from $A$ at $60^\circ$: $D=t(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2)$; the circle equation gives $t^2-12t=0$, so $t=12$ and $D=(6,6\sqrt3)$ (so $ACD$ is equilateral). Then $E=(0,6\sqrt3)$ and $F=(6,0)$.

Line $DF$ is $x=6$, through the center, so $H=(6,-2\sqrt3)$ and $FH=2\sqrt3$.

Line $EF$: $y=6\sqrt3-\sqrt3x$. Substituting into $(x-6)^2+(y-2\sqrt3)^2=48$ gives $x^2-9x+9=0$, $x=\frac{9\pm3\sqrt5}2$. The point on the minor arc $AC$ (below the $x$-axis, so $y<0$, i.e. $x>6$) is $x_J=\frac{9+3\sqrt5}2$, at horizontal distance $x_J-6=\frac{3(\sqrt5-1)}2$ from line $FH$.

$[FHJ]=\frac12\cdot FH\cdot(x_J-6)=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt3\cdot\frac{3(\sqrt5-1)}2=\frac32(\sqrt{15}-\sqrt3)$.

So $a=3,b=2,c=15,d=3$ (any other representation, e.g. $\frac34(\sqrt{60}-\sqrt{12})$, has a larger sum) and the answer is $23$.

**Answer: 23**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-07.title: Area ratios
pumac-2018-geometry-b-07.body:
The triangle is acute ($11^2<9^2+10^2$), so $O$ is inside and $D,E,F$ lie on the sides. For a point $P$ inside the triangle with cevians through $A,B,C$ meeting the opposite sides at $D,E,F$:
$$\frac{PD}{AD}=\frac{[PBC]}{[ABC]},\ \ \frac{PE}{BE}=\frac{[PCA]}{[ABC]},\ \ \frac{PF}{CF}=\frac{[PAB]}{[ABC]},$$
which add to $1$. Since $\frac{PA}{AD}=1-\frac{PD}{AD}$ etc., $\frac{PA}{AD}+\frac{PB}{BE}+\frac{PC}{CF}=3-1=2$.

For $P=O$ we have $OA=OB=OC=R$, so $R\left(\frac1{AD}+\frac1{BE}+\frac1{CF}\right)=2$. The area is $\sqrt{15\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4}=30\sqrt2$, so $R=\frac{9\cdot10\cdot11}{4\cdot30\sqrt2}=\frac{33\sqrt2}8$. Hence the sum is $\frac2R=\frac{16}{33\sqrt2}=\frac{8\sqrt2}{33}$, and $a+b+c=8+2+33=43$.

**Answer: 43**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-08.title: Coordinates
pumac-2018-geometry-b-08.body:
Since $BD\perp BC$, $BD=\sqrt{35^2-28^2}=21$. Take $B=(0,0)$, $C=(28,0)$, $D=(0,21)$, so $A=B+D-C=(-28,21)$.

The directions from $A$ to $B$ and $D$ are $(\frac45,-\frac35)$ and $(1,0)$; their sum $(\frac95,-\frac35)\parallel(3,-1)$ is the bisector direction. Direction of $AC$: $(8,-3)$. Reflecting in the axis $\mathbf a=(3,-1)$: $2\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a}{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a}\mathbf a-\mathbf v=\frac{27}5(3,-1)-(8,-3)=\left(\frac{41}5,-\frac{12}5\right)\parallel(41,-12)$. So $\ell_1:(-28+41t,\ 21-12t)$.

$CD$ has direction $(-4,3)$, so $\ell_2$ through $B$ has direction $(3,4)$: $(3s,4s)$. Solving $-28+41t=3s$, $21-12t=4s$ gives $t=\frac78$, so $P=\left(\frac{63}8,\frac{21}2\right)$.

Then $PD=\left|\left(\frac{63}8,\frac{21}2-21\right)\right|=\frac{21}8|(3,-4)|=\frac{105}8$, and $m+n=105+8=113$.

**Answer: 113**

pumac-2018-geometry-b-08.title: Symmedian argument
pumac-2018-geometry-b-08.body:
The diagonals bisect each other, so $AC$ passes through the midpoint $M$ of $BD$ and is the median of $\triangle ABD$ from $A$; its reflection in the bisector of $\angle BAD$ is the symmedian from $A$. The symmedian, the perpendicular bisector of $BD$ and the tangents to the circumcircle of $ABD$ at $B$ and $D$ are concurrent, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BD$ and $PD$ is tangent to that circumcircle at $D$.

Triangle $ABD$ has $BD\perp AD$ (as $AD\parallel BC$), with $AD=28$, $BD=21$, $AB=35$. By the tangent-chord angle, $\angle PDM=\angle DAB$, so $\cos\angle PDM=\frac{28}{35}=\frac45$ and $PD=\dfrac{DM}{\cos\angle PDM}=\dfrac{21/2}{4/5}=\dfrac{105}8$.

**Answer: 113**
